input:
Case

This proposal requests approval to proceed to detailed design for a water recycling plant. It is important to clarify at the outset that the decision requested at this stage is design approval only: construction is not being requested, and no contractor is named anywhere in this proposal.

The plant would serve a site that currently takes its process water from the mains supply and discharges its used water after treatment. A recycling plant effectively closes part of that loop on the site itself: used water that currently leaves as discharge is treated to the standard the process requires and returned to service. The case for the plant essentially rests on the two flows it displaces. Every unit of water that is recycled is a unit not drawn from the mains and a unit not discharged, and the site's exposure to supply interruption and to discharge consent limits is reduced by the same movement. The case is stated at the level this proposal can support: the recycling route is technically standard, the treatment steps it requires are established practice, and the question the proposal needs to answer is not whether the water can be recycled but rather what the plant costs, how it is built into a working site, and what approval is being asked for now.

The proposal therefore places the decision in its proper position. Detailed design converts the concept into a priced, scheduled construction package; it is also the stage at which the remaining uncertainties in the scheme are priced rather than merely described. Approving detailed design commits the project to that design work and to nothing beyond it. The construction decision will follow on the detailed design, with its own case, its own costs and its own approval.

Costs

The capital cost is $1116k. This figure is a proposal-stage estimate for the complete plant: the treatment process itself, the civils and building work the plant requires, installation and tie-ins to the existing water and discharge systems, and commissioning. The appraisal horizon for the project is 10 years, and the capital figure is the cost on which the appraisal is run.

The estimate is stated at the accuracy that a proposal-stage figure carries. It is built up from the process design as it currently stands, from vendor indications for the principal equipment, and from the site's own rates for civils and installation; it is not a tender price, and no contractor has priced the work. Detailed design is the stage that firms up the figure: it fixes the equipment list, the tie-in points and the construction sequence, and it returns a cost on which the construction decision can be taken. Operating cost is carried in the appraisal qualitatively at this stage, as the plant's energy, chemical and labour demands depend on the equipment choices made in detailed design; the appraisal structure is set now so that those figures can enter it without rebuilding the case when they become known. The $1116k is held as the single capital figure of this proposal, and any change to it belongs to the detailed design report, stated together with its reasons.

Schedule

The project is scheduled to start one quarter after approval. The schedule is stated from that start point in sequence, because the dates that matter to the site are the order of the stages and the points at which the working site is affected, and both of these follow from the sequence rather than from a calendar fixed in advance of approval.

Detailed design comes first, and it ends at a defined point: a priced construction package and a construction schedule that the site can plan around. Procurement follows design, with the long-lead treatment equipment ordered against the specifications produced by the detailed design. Construction and installation follow procurement, and these are the stages that touch the operating site: tie-ins to the water and discharge systems are made in planned windows, and the existing systems continue running outside those windows. Commissioning closes the sequence: the plant is proved on the site's actual used water, at the site's actual demand, before being handed over as a working part of the water system. Each stage starts from the completed output of the stage before it, and the approval requested here covers the first stage only; later stages will return for their own approvals as their costs become firm.

Decision requested

The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design for the water recycling plant, on the capital basis of $1116k and the 10-year appraisal horizon stated in this proposal. The approval commits the project to the detailed design work: the process design completed to construction standard, the equipment list fixed and priced, the tie-ins engineered, and a construction cost and schedule returned for a separate construction decision. It does not commit the project to construction, and it authorises no construction spending whatsoever.

The design stage carries its own discipline. It reports against this proposal: the capital figure it returns is compared with the figure approved here, item by item, and a movement in either direction is explained by the design work that produced it. The stage does not expand the plant's scope on its own authority; a larger or smaller plant than the one proposed is a change of case, and it returns with the construction decision rather than inside it.

Two features of the ask are deliberate. The ask is made at the point where the remaining uncertainties are matters of price and programme, which detailed design exists to settle; seeking construction approval now would price those uncertainties as contingency instead of resolving them. And the ask names its own boundary: if detailed design returns a materially different capital figure, or a construction sequence that the site cannot accept, the construction case will come back as a new decision, rather than as an extension of this one. The steering decision is therefore a bounded one: approve the design stage, on the stated basis, and receive in return the priced package on which the full decision can properly be taken.
